content: 1. Acting on a report, evidence, and recommendations is distinct from reporting potential child abuse exposure in the home to child welfare authorities. 2. The World Health Organization (WHO) publication Preventing Child Maltreatment: A Guide to Taking Action and Generating Evidence (2006) by authors Butchart A, Harvey A, Mian M, and Furniss T provides a framework for addressing child maltreatment. 3. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) identified significant knowledge gaps that require further research. Many recommendations in the guidelines are based on evidence of very low or low quality, highlighting the need for additional studies. 4. Even in areas with higher-quality evidence, certain aspects of the topic lack sufficient research data. 5. The GDG identified specific research gaps during their review of the draft guidelines. These gaps do not represent a comprehensive assessment but highlight areas requiring further investigation. 6. Research is needed to assess the clinical and cost-effectiveness of clinical inquiry or case-finding compared to universal screening in improving outcomes across various settings, such as general practice, antenatal care, family planning, trauma and emergency care, HIV clinics, substance abuse clinics, and mental health-care settings. 7. The role of intimate partner violence (IPV), including coercion, in reproductive decision-making and health outcomes should be explored. 8. Trials with adequate statistical power are necessary to evaluate the effectiveness of different psychological interventions or therapies for women survivors of IPV in diverse settings, including primary care and emergency departments. 9. The potential benefits of support groups, particularly in communal settings, should be investigated. 10. Advocacy and support interventions need to be tested in settings outside antenatal care in high-income countries, with a focus on ensuring women's safety. 11. Interventions to prevent the intergenerational transmission of IPV are required, as this phenomenon is common. 12. Studies on care for mothers and children exposed to IPV are lacking, especially in low-income settings. 13. Home visitation trials, similar to those used for child maltreatment, should include a focus on women experiencing IPV and measure IPV as a primary outcome. 14. Mother-child interventions proven effective in high-income settings should be studied in low-resource settings, with alternatives to intensive psychotherapy identified and further evaluated. 15. Safe shelter options should be evaluated, particularly in resource-poor settings. 16. For survivors of sexual assault, there is a need for studies on psychological interventions specific to this population, allowing subgroup analysis and addressing common co-morbidities. 17. The provision of cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) by non-specialists and the delivery of CBT in different contexts should be evaluated. 18. A randomized controlled trial is needed to determine whether treating Trichomonas infection improves adherence to other medications, as the treatment is unpleasant but not life-threatening. 19. Research should establish the minimum content and duration of training on IPV and sexual violence for health-care providers to improve their skills. 20. Cost-effective methods for providing in-service training in lowand middle-income countries, such as ongoing education, should be investigated. 21. Rigorous evaluation of successful service delivery programs is necessary to assess their applicability in other settings. 22. More research on Sexual Assault Nurse Examiner (SANE) programs is encouraged, particularly regarding their integration into health-care settings in lowand middle-income countries. 23. Standard models of care, such as those for chronic conditions, should be adapted and evaluated for survivors of IPV and sexual assault. 24. Research should address the unique considerations in delivering services to adolescents exposed to violence. 25. Dissemination and implementation of the guidelines aim to improve care quality and health outcomes related to violence against women. 26. WHO has adopted a formal knowledge-to-action framework for disseminating, adapting, and implementing guidelines, supported by a list of priority actions. 27. The guidelines will be disseminated through WHO offices, ministries of health, collaborating centers, professional associations, UN agencies, NGOs, and the WHO website. 28. A policy brief targeting policymakers, program managers, and clinicians will be developed and distributed through WHO country offices and partners. 29. Successful integration of evidence-based policies into national programs and health-care services requires well-planned, participatory processes of adaptation and implementation. 30. Recommendations should be adapted into locally appropriate documents, considering available human and financial resources. 31. Modifications should be limited to conditional recommendations, with explicit and transparent justification for any changes. 32. A framework should be established to create an enabling environment for using the recommendations and supporting health-care practitioners in evidence-based practices. 33. Local professional societies play a crucial role, and an inclusive, participatory process should be encouraged. 34. Implementation of the recommendations should ideally be monitored at the health-facility level using clinical audits or criterion-based audits to track changes in care for women survivors of violence. 35. Clear review criteria and monitoring indicators should be defined and associated with locally agreed targets. 36. The WHO compendium Violence Against Women and Girls: A Compendium of Monitoring and Evaluation Indicators provides a comprehensive list of indicators for health programs addressing violence against women and girls. 37. Suggested indicators include the number of medical and allied health faculties implementing training on IPV and sexual violence, changes in national guidelines, and the proportion of health-care providers trained in IPV prevalence and consequences. 38. Other indicators include the proportion of women survivors receiving first-line emotional support, undergoing danger assessments, and accessing emergency contraception and psychological support within 72 hours of sexual assault. 39. Health services should conduct institution-wide assessments of policies, protocols, and practices related to violence against women, including privacy, confidentiality, training gaps, and resource availability. 40. The Danger Assessment tool, which evaluates the risk of an abused woman being killed by her partner, has not been tested in lowand middle-income countries. 41. The guidelines will be updated in five years or sooner if new evidence necessitates changes. WHO welcomes suggestions for additional questions to include in future guidelines.
